intro: Every long story is heading somewhere. In this last unit you read the ancient texts about where the Bible's story ends. Psalm 82 puts the gods of the nations on trial. Daniel 7 gives a kingdom to the holy ones. Paul calls believers adopted children and heirs. Revelation ends with a battle, a bound dragon, and a garden city whose gates never shut.

You will read the documents first: the Hebrew Bible and the Septuagint, a Dead Sea Scroll, Jubilees and 1 Enoch in R. H. Charles's 1917 translation, the New Testament, and church fathers such as Justin, Irenaeus, Athanasius and Augustine. Then you will meet the researchers who read them: Mullen and Smith on the divine council, Collins on Daniel, Clifford on the holy mountain, Beale and Bauckham on Revelation, and Michael Heiser on God's family and Har Magedon.

By the end you will be able to explain what these texts promise the people they call children of God, and why readers of every tradition say those people never become equal to God. You will be able to trace a word from Hebrew into Greek, compare a symbol with its older source, and describe a debate fairly without taking a side.
bigQuestion: What do the ancient texts say about the end of the story, from God's children raised to honor to the nations healed, and how do different readers understand them?

timeline.t: Pharaoh Thutmose III wins a battle at Megiddo, recorded at Karnak
King Josiah of Judah dies at Megiddo facing Pharaoh Necho (2 Kings 23:29)
The book of Daniel takes its final form, by many scholars' dating
Jubilees is written, telling of spirits set over the nations
Paul writes Romans, with its chapter on adoption and creation's hope
Revelation is written, by many scholars' dating, naming Har Magedon
Justin Martyr's Dialogue with Trypho expects a thousand years in Jerusalem
Irenaeus writes Against Heresies, quoting 'I said, Ye are gods'
Athanasius writes On the Incarnation, a key text for theosis
Augustine finishes The City of God, reading the thousand years as the church's age
Gregory Palamas distinguishes God's essence and energies
The first Dead Sea Scrolls are found in caves near Qumran

words.d: the gathering of heavenly beings around God's throne, which many scholars see in Psalm 82
the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures; it reads 'angels of God' in Deuteronomy 32:8
the holy ones who receive the kingdom in Daniel 7; readers debate whether they are human, heavenly or both
taking someone into a family as a child with full rights; Paul's picture for becoming God's child
a person with the right to receive a parent's property or position
a Hebrew word for God, gods or heavenly beings, depending on the passage
the Eastern Orthodox teaching of sharing God's life by grace, never his essence
Hebrew for 'mount of assembly,' named in Isaiah 14:13
a mound made of layers of ruined towns, like Megiddo
the cube-shaped inner room of the temple, where God's presence was said to dwell
writing that reveals hidden realities through visions and symbols, as in Daniel and Revelation

test.q: What does Jubilees 15 say God set over the nations other than Israel?
test.why: Jubilees 15 (Charles, 1917) says God placed spirits over the nations but ruled Israel himself.

test.q: Which ancient witnesses read 'sons of God' or 'angels of God' in Deuteronomy 32:8?
choices: The Masoretic Text and the Mishnah
The Latin Vulgate and the KJV
A Qumran scroll and the Septuagint
test.why: A Dead Sea Scroll reads 'sons of God' and the Septuagint 'angels of God'; the Masoretic Text reads 'sons of Israel.'

test.q: What does John 1:12 say those who received him were given?
choices: The keys to the bottomless pit
Power, or the right, to become sons of God
test.why: John 1:12 says they were given power, or the right, to become the sons of God.
Romans 8:23 speaks of waiting for the adoption, the redemption of the body.

test.q: In 1 Corinthians 6:3, what does Paul say believers will do?
test.why: Paul asks, 'Know ye not that we shall judge angels?'

test.q: Which psalm does Jesus quote in John 10:34?
test.why: Jesus quotes Psalm 82:6, 'I said, Ye are gods.'

test.q: How does Orthodox theosis differ from becoming God?
choices: Humans replace God on his throne
Humans share God's life by grace, never his essence
test.why: Orthodox teaching says humans share God's energies by grace, never his essence.

test.q: Which verse calls Israel God's son, his firstborn?
test.why: Exodus 4:22 says Israel is God's son, his firstborn.

test.q: Which text promises the righteous they will be companions of the hosts of heaven?
test.why: 1 Enoch 104 (Charles, 1917) promises the righteous they will shine and join the hosts of heaven.

test.q: Why do some scholars doubt that Har Magedon means Mount Megiddo?
choices: Megiddo is a mound on a plain, never called a mountain
test.why: Megiddo is a tel on a plain, and no Hebrew Bible text calls it a mountain.

test.q: In Heiser's reading, where is the final battle really aimed?
choices: At God's mountain, Zion, the mount of assembly
test.why: Heiser read the battle as the powers' last stand against God's council mountain, Zion.

test.q: Which two place names show Greek writing ayin as g?
test.why: Hebrew 'Amorah and 'Azzah became Greek Gomorrha and Gaza.

test.q: What does Revelation 22:2 say the leaves of the tree of life are for?
test.why: Revelation 22:2 says the leaves are for the healing of the nations.

test.q: Which approach reads Revelation as timeless truths rather than particular events?
test.why: The idealist approach reads Revelation as pictures of timeless truths.

test.q: Which Hebrew Bible room shares the new Jerusalem's cube shape?
test.why: 1 Kings 6:20 gives the holy of holies equal length, width and height.

write.prompt: What do the ancient texts say about the future of the people they call God's children or holy ones? Choose two or three passages from this unit (for example Psalm 82:6–8, Daniel 7:27, 1 Corinthians 6:3, 1 Enoch 104, Revelation 3:21 or 22:2). Explain what each text says, then how at least two readers or traditions read it, such as a church father, a Jewish reading, Heiser, Collins or Bauckham.
tips: Start with the document: name each text by book, chapter and verse, and say which translation you used.
Attribute every reading: Collins argues, Orthodox teaching says, Heiser reads, many commentators hold.
Compare readings side by side; do not rank them or say which is true.
Use the unit's terms, such as divine council, adoption, har mo'ed and theosis, and explain each one.
Describe modern scholars' ideas in your own words; their books are not quoted.
